title: The Necrotizing Fasciitis Survivor Whose Heart Gave Way Six Years Later

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is 46 years old. Six years before this admission, a thorn prick in his left foot led to swelling that turned out to be necrotizing fasciitis, severe enough to require dialysis — four or five sessions of hemodialysis at the time. After that, he recovered and stayed well for six years.

Then, 20 days before this admission, both legs began swelling, along with abdominal distension and shortness of breath — all insidious in onset and gradually worsening, though the breathlessness eased somewhat with medication. He was referred on for further evaluation. He has a history of hypothyroidism and hypertension, the latter on irregular medication.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: conscious, coherent, cooperative
- Local findings: pitting pedal edema present for 20 days; distended abdomen with a central, inverted umbilicus, no engorged veins or visible pulsation
- Vitals: afebrile, pulse 84 bpm, blood pressure 160/100 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air
- Cardiovascular exam: jugular venous pressure not elevated, no parasternal heave, apex beat felt 0.5 cm lateral to the mid-clavicular line in the 6th intercostal space; heart sounds normal, no murmurs
- Abdominal exam: dullness on percussion over the flanks with shifting dullness and a fluid thrill, consistent with ascites; soft, non-tender, no organomegaly; bowel sounds present
- Respiratory exam: bilateral air entry, normal vesicular breathing
- Neurological exam: higher mental functions normal, no focal deficit
- Investigations sent: blood counts and biochemistry panels, liver and renal function tests, and further imaging (documented but not detailed in the available record)

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
His working diagnosis brought together several threads: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as part of a type 4 cardiorenal syndrome, alongside dilated cardiomyopathy and ischemic hepatitis. He was started on furosemide, isosorbide dinitrate, sodium bicarbonate (nodosis), iron and calcium supplementation, and dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel, plus a statin.

By the next day, metoprolol was added to his regimen for further cardiac support, and his treatment plan remained stable through the following day of documented care — a multi-drug regimen addressing his heart failure, renal impairment, and background metabolic conditions together, reflecting how his six-year-old necrotizing fasciitis and hemodialysis history had set the stage for this more complex re-presentation.
